title: Car skids or slides too easily
h1: Why does my car skid or hydroplane so easily?
metaDesc: Car hydroplanes, skids or slides more than it should? See the likely causes, from worn tires to ABS problems, and what to check first.
intro: If you're in a skid right now: take your foot off the gas, look and steer where you want to go, and don't slam the brakes. Our roadside page on skids and hydroplaning has the step-by-step version. Once you're safely stopped, this guide helps you work out why the car slid, from worn or low tires to anti-lock brake (ABS) or traction control problems.
safety: If you're sliding now: ease off the gas, look where you want to go and steer there. If you need to brake and the car has anti-lock brakes (ABS), press firmly and hold. Without ABS, pump the brakes if the wheels start to lock.
If the car went off the road or stopped in a traffic lane, turn on your hazard lights. If anyone is hurt or you're stuck in a lane, call 911.
If a tire is flat, bulging, or has cords or wires showing, don't drive on it. Use the spare or call for help.
If the brake pedal feels soft or the red BRAKE light is on, don't drive until the brakes are checked.

q_tires.q: With the car parked, look at your tires. Which fits best?
q_tires.help: Penny test: put a penny upside down into a tread groove. If you can see all of Lincoln's head, NHTSA says the tires need replacing.

opts.a: A tire looks low, flat or bulging, or has cords or wires showing
The tread looks worn: smooth, or I can see all of Lincoln's head in the penny test
I'm not sure, or I can't check right now
On wet roads, especially at highway speed: it feels like floating
When I brake: the wheels lock up or the car slides
When I turn or speed up: the back end steps out or the wheels spin

q_winter.q: What kind of tires are on the car?
q_winter.help: The tire's sidewall may say M+S (all-season) or show a mountain with a snowflake (winter-rated).

opts.a: Winter or snow tires, and it still slides a lot

q_abs.q: Is the ABS light or the traction control light on?

opts.a: Yes, one or both are on
No lights, but I hear the tires screech or feel the wheels lock up
No lights, and the pedal buzzes or pulses when I brake hard on slippery roads

result.title: A low or damaged tire can make the car slide and may fail
result.now: Don't drive on it. If you're safely off the road and know how, put on the spare. Otherwise call roadside assistance.
if: If the tire is just low with no damage, inflate it to the pressure on the driver's door sticker, then have it checked for a leak soon.
If the car pulls hard to one side or shakes, have the tire and wheel checked before driving far.
result.why: A tire that's low, bulging or worn through has far less grip and can blow out. Low pressure also lets the tire squirm and float on water more easily.

causes.name: Low pressure or a slow leak
causes.clues: One tire looks lower than the others, or the tire pressure light is on.

causes.name: Sidewall bulge or damage
causes.clues: You hit a pothole or curb recently.

causes.name: Tread worn through to the cords
causes.clues: You can see threads or wires in the tread.

you: Check the pressure with a gauge against the door sticker, not the number on the tire.

result.title: Worn tires are the most likely reason the car slides
result.now: Replace worn tires within the next few days. Until then, slow down well below the limit on wet or snowy roads and leave extra space.
if: If the tread is down to the wear bars or any cords show, don't drive on it.
If you're only replacing two tires, ask the shop which end of the car they should go on.
result.why: Tread grooves push water out from under the tire. As tread wears down, the tire can't clear water fast enough and starts to ride on top of it, which is hydroplaning. Worn tires also grip much less on snow and ice. NHTSA says to keep at least 2/32 of an inch of tread on all tires.

causes.name: Worn tread
causes.clues: The penny test shows all of Lincoln's head.

causes.name: Uneven wear
causes.clues: One edge of the tire is much more worn than the other.

causes.name: Old, hardened tires
causes.clues: Small cracks in the sidewall, or tires that are many years old.

you: Do the penny test in several grooves on each tire.
Look for wear bars that are level with the tread.
shop: Alignment check if the wear is uneven

result.title: Water on the road plus speed is the usual cause of hydroplaning
result.now: Check the tread with the penny test and set the tire pressures to the driver's door sticker. On wet roads, slow down, stay out of puddles and standing water, and don't use cruise control.
if: If the tread is low or the tires are old, replace them soon.
If one tire keeps losing air, have it checked for a leak.
result.why: At higher speeds, water can build up under the tires faster than the tread can push it away, and the tires lose contact with the road. Slower speeds, good tread and the right pressure all help the tires stay on the road.

causes.name: Speed too high for the rain
causes.clues: It happened at highway speed or in heavy rain.

causes.name: Tread lower than it looks
causes.clues: The penny test is close.

causes.name: Low tire pressure
causes.clues: A tire looks low, or the tire pressure light is on.

causes.name: Deep standing water or ruts
causes.clues: It happened in a puddle or a worn lane.

you: Check all four pressures, cold, against the door sticker.
shop: Tread depth and tire condition check

result.title: All-season and summer tires have limited grip on snow and ice
result.now: Slow down a lot on snow and ice and leave much more space to stop. If you often drive in snow, think about winter tires.
if: If they're summer or performance tires, avoid snow and ice. They get hard and slippery in the cold.
Check tire pressure often in cold weather. NHTSA notes that it drops as temperatures fall.
result.why: Tires made for warm or mild weather get harder in the cold, and their tread isn't designed to bite into snow. Even good all-season tires have far less grip on snow and ice than on dry roads, so speed and stopping distance matter most.

causes.name: Tire type
causes.clues: Summer or all-season tires, and it slides mostly in snow.

causes.name: Worn tread
causes.clues: The penny test is close.

causes.name: Low pressure in the cold
causes.clues: A tire pressure light on cold mornings.

you: Check the tire sidewall for M+S or a mountain-and-snowflake symbol.

result.title: The anti-lock brakes (ABS) or stability control may be switched off by a fault
result.now: Get the ABS codes read within the next few days. Until then, brake earlier, leave extra room and slow down on slippery roads.
if: If the red BRAKE light is on too, or the pedal feels soft, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
If the traction light shows the word OFF, the button may have been pressed. Press it again or restart the car.
result.why: Anti-lock brakes stop the wheels from locking so you can still steer while braking hard. Traction and stability control help stop wheelspin and slides. When a fault switches them off, the light comes on and the car can slide more easily, though the normal brakes still work.

causes.name: Faulty wheel speed sensor or wire
causes.clues: It started after a pothole, brake work or wet, salty weather.

causes.name: ABS unit fault
causes.clues: Several brake-related lights are on.

causes.name: Traction control switched off
causes.clues: The light says OFF.

you: Note which lights are on and whether any say OFF.
shop: ABS and stability control code scan

result.title: The wheels may be locking because the anti-lock brakes aren't working, or the car doesn't have them
result.now: Have the brakes and ABS checked within the next few days. Until then, brake earlier and more gently, especially on wet or slippery roads.
if: If the car pulls hard to one side when braking, or the pedal feels soft, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
If your car doesn't have ABS, pump the brakes if the wheels start to lock, as NHTSA advises.
result.why: Most newer cars have anti-lock brakes that keep the wheels turning in a hard stop. If the wheels lock and skid with no ABS light, the system may not be working, the car may not have it, or worn tires may be letting go before ABS can help.

causes.name: ABS not working
causes.clues: The wheels lock and screech even with gentle braking on wet roads.

causes.name: Car without ABS
causes.clues: An older or basic car, and no ABS light at startup.

causes.name: Worn tires
causes.clues: The penny test is close.

causes.name: One brake grabbing
causes.clues: The car pulls to one side when you brake.

you: Watch whether the ABS light comes on for a moment when you start the car.
shop: ABS code scan and function test

result.title: That buzzing or pulsing is the anti-lock brakes doing their job
result.now: When you feel it, keep firm, steady pressure on the pedal and don't pump it. A slide means the road is slippery, so slow down and leave more space.
if: If you feel pulsing on dry roads, or the ABS light comes on, have the brakes checked.
If the tires are worn, replacing them will help more than anything else.
result.why: On slippery roads, ABS quickly pulses the brakes to stop the wheels from locking. You feel it as buzzing or pulsing in the pedal. NHTSA says that with ABS you should press firmly and hold the pedal.

causes.name: Normal ABS action on a slippery road
causes.clues: It happens only on wet, icy or loose roads.

causes.name: Worn tires
causes.clues: The penny test is close.

causes.name: Speed too high for conditions
causes.clues: It happens when braking from higher speeds.

you: Do the penny test on each tire.
shop: Brake and ABS check if it happens on dry roads

result.title: Tires, traction control or a heavy foot may be letting the wheels spin or the rear slide
result.now: Make sure traction and stability control are on (no OFF light) and check the tire pressures. Speed up and turn more gently on slippery roads, and book a tire and alignment check.
if: If the rear tires are much more worn than the fronts, replace them soon. Worn rear tires make the back end slide.
If the car wanders or pulls even on dry roads, have the steering and suspension checked soon.
If the traction control light stays on, it may be off because of a fault. Have it checked.
result.why: Wheelspin and a sliding rear end usually come from too much gas for the grip available, tires that don't match or are worn, or traction control that's switched off. Worn suspension or bad alignment can make it worse.

causes.name: Traction or stability control off
causes.clues: An OFF light on the dash.

causes.name: Worn or mismatched tires
causes.clues: The rear tires are more worn, or the tires are different brands or sizes.

causes.name: Too much gas on slippery roads
causes.clues: It happens when pulling away or speeding up in turns.

causes.name: Worn suspension or bad alignment
causes.clues: The car wanders, or the tires wear unevenly.

you: Compare the tread on the front and rear tires.

result.title: Have the tires, brakes and traction systems checked
result.now: Have the tires, alignment and brakes checked within the next few days. Until then, slow down on wet or slippery roads and leave extra space.
if: If any warning light comes on, or the brakes feel different, get it checked sooner.
If a tire looks low or damaged, don't drive on it.
result.why: A car that slides more than it should usually has a tire problem, is going too fast for the conditions, or has an anti-lock brake or traction control fault. A shop can check all three quickly.

causes.name: Tires
causes.clues: Low tread, low pressure or old tires.

causes.name: Speed for the conditions
causes.clues: It happens in rain, snow or on curves.

causes.name: ABS or traction control fault
causes.clues: A warning light is on.

you: Do the penny test and check the pressures.
shop: ABS and stability control code scan
